newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Post-budget rate speculation buoys sterling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Post-budget rate speculation buoys sterling.

text.p: Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's annual budget statement failed to dispel the idea that lending rates will have to rise again soon, giving sterling another boost on Wednesday, financial analysts said.

"Forget about the tax and spending measures, the bottom line for the financial markets is - "Has he done enough to stop interest rates going up?' - answer no," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
While generally seen as a cautious annual fiscal package, most see Clarke's tax giveaways as adding fuel to the consumer spending inflation fire.
While the fiscal stimulus from tax cuts seems modest, the expenditure reductions appear exaggerated, said Paul Lambert, currency economist at UBS.

He noted the futures market had already taken account of a potential base rate increase of between 0.75 and 1.0 percentage points by the end of 1997 as a means of dampening consumer demand. Base rates are currently 6.0 percent.
With the hawkish Bank of England almost certain to continue to call for further monetary tightening, analysts said what was important now was if Clarke himself thought policy was tight enough.
Despite the new era of more policy openness and tiny steps towards central bank independence, the Chancellor still has the ultimate power to veto Bank of England governor Eddie George.
Analysts latched on to Clarke's comment in the budget that he wanted a tight fiscal policy in order to reduce the risk of having to tighten monetary policy excessively.
Coleman said the word excessively was interesting. It suggests he is still thinking about putting rates up and might have to.
Sterling will also continue to benefit from its safe-haven status amid lingering concern that there could be turmoil in other European markets in the run up to economic and monetary union (EMU).
Britain is seen as being the least likely of the mainstream European countries to join the first round of EMU in 1999.
The latest J.P. Morgan calculator, which shows the probability of countries participating in EMU, has Britain on only a 38 percent chance compared with Italy at 62 percent and France at 100 percent.
Expectations of additional rate hikes will ensure that the pound continues to benefit from investors wishing to hold currencies likely to remain aloof from the EMU process, UBS's Lambert said.
This may be particularly true of investors in Japan and Switzerland, where money market interest rates remain near record low levels.
Despite the interest rate prop keeping sterling on a firmer tack, analysts warned that the upside is probably fairly limited given its bumper 12 percent overall rise this year.
According to the latest global investor survey by Merrill Lynch, fund managers reporting overweight currency exposure in sterling rose sharply to record levels in November.

"Heavily overweight sterling readings from our Global Investor Survey and extreme bullishness on market sentiment indicators show sterling/dollar may be close to an interim top," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.
Since the Chancellor ended his budget speech on Tuesday, the pound has risen over half a pfennig and half a cent to 2.56 marks and $1.6800.
